frenchVerbParadigms.explanation: Source English 'to eat'; source example 'I don't eat meat.' = card 12 and Reader line 4. Slot alignment: yo→je, tú→tu, él_ella→il (also elle/on), nosotros→nous, ellos→ils (also elles). The source has no slot for French 'vous'; the usted and ustedes readings of the source's third-person slots correspond to 'vous' (mangez). Spelling: 'nous mangeons' keeps the e. The source note 'put no right before the verb' does not transfer: French negation wraps the verb (ne … pas), and du/de la/des become 'de' after negation (pas de viande).

Source English 'to be (state, readiness)'; source example 'We're not ready yet.' = card 14 and Reader line 3. Same slot alignment as manger; usted/ustedes correspond to 'vous êtes', as in Reader line 2. French has one verb 'être' for both Spanish ser and estar. 'Prêt' agrees in gender and number: prêt, prête, prêts, prêtes.

Mapping note: the source glosses tener as 'to have', whose literal French counterpart is 'avoir'. The source example 'The corn tortillas don't have gluten.' is Reader line 8, which French renders with 'contiennent', so this slot gives 'contenir' to match the French the learner actually reads. Same slot alignment as manger; 'ils' form is the one used in Reader lines 7 and 8. 'Contenir' conjugates like 'tenir': stem 'contien-' except 'nous contenons' and 'vous contenez', which parallels the source note on tener's stem change. The example line is under owner hold (see residuals).

Source English 'to use'; source example 'I'm going to ask the kitchen if they use nuts or peanuts.' = Reader line 6. Regular -er verb; 'je' elides to 'j'utilise'. Same slot alignment as manger. The source 'usan' (ellos/ustedes) is 'ils utilisent' in Reader line 6, where 'they' means the kitchen staff; addressed to staff directly it would be 'vous utilisez'.

internalDomainNotes: Internal only, not learner-facing. This is a language lesson and must not be presented as allergy or dietary guidance.

Lactose-free milk is cow's milk with the lactose broken down or removed. It still contains milk proteins (casein, whey), so it is a dairy product and is unsafe for someone with a milk-protein allergy. It suits lactose intolerance only.

The source does not say why Tom avoids dairy; his only stated allergy is peanuts. The lactose-free milk in line 9 is Emma's order. A learner could still infer that lactose-free milk suits someone avoiding dairy, which is false for milk allergy.

Reader line 7 (green chilaquiles without cream or cheese have no meat or dairy) is unverified and may be unsafe as stated. Salsa verde can be made with chicken stock, the tortilla chips can be fried in lard or shared oil, and garnishes or cross-contact can add dairy. Luis asserts it without checking with the kitchen.

Reader line 8 (corn tortillas don't have gluten) is unverified and may be unsafe as stated. Some tortillas are corn-wheat blends, and cross-contact can occur on shared surfaces, presses or fryers. This matters for coeliac disease and wheat allergy.

Peanuts are legumes, not tree nuts, and the two are separate allergens; a person may react to one, the other or both. EU labelling lists 'arachides' and 'fruits à coque' as separate categories. The French keeps them as separate terms.

In Mexican Spanish, 'nuez' often means pecan or walnut specifically, so 'nueces' in line 6 may be narrower than a full tree-nut question. 'Fruits à coque' follows the broader source English 'nuts'. In a real setting, the question would need to name the specific allergen.
In line 6 Luis says he will ask the kitchen; the source never gives the answer. The Reader does not establish that any dish is safe for Tom.
In any real setting, ingredients and cross-contact must be confirmed with staff.

sourceNotes: Direction is French→English: French is the learner's native/input language and English is the target/output language. All six modes prompt in French and elicit the exact source English. The critique's proposal to invert the modes (prompt English, elicit French) is rejected.

The source is unchanged. The 17 English cards and 9 English Reader lines keep their source order and wording; forms and modes quote the source English exactly. Oaxaca, Luis, Emma and Tom are preserved, and all nine Reader claims appear in source sequence.
The speaking objective is the source task verbatim as a single item, restoring the sequence the earlier candidate had split into three paraphrases.

Card 2 and Reader line 6: source 'the nuts' / 'las nueces' is rendered 'les fruits à coque', the broad French term in an allergy context, instead of 'les noix', which mainly means walnuts. Caveat: Spanish 'nueces' may itself be narrower than English 'nuts' (see internalDomainNotes), so the French follows the source English.

Card 3: the source note says 'cacahuate' is the Mexican word ('maní' elsewhere). French uses 'cacahuète'; 'arachide' is the usual labelling term. Peanuts are kept separate from 'fruits à coque' throughout.

Card 6 and Reader lines 4 and 9: it is Emma who orders lactose-free milk in line 9, while Tom is the one who does not eat dairy in line 4. The card 6 note says this and adds that lactose-free milk is still a dairy product.
Cards 7 and 8 are given as 'ne … personne' and 'ne … pas encore', because bare 'personne' reads as the noun 'a person'.
Card 9: the source note warns against Spanish 'un otro'. French, unlike Spanish, keeps the article (un autre café, une autre tasse); the earlier gender-agreement framing is dropped.

Cards 10 and 16: phrase-initial 'Plus de lait' can be read as 'no more milk', so card 16 uses 'Davantage de lait' and card 10 lists both 'plus de' and 'davantage de'. Reader line 9 keeps 'avec plus de', which is unambiguous.
Card 13: the source note 'A woman says alérgica' has no French equivalent change; 'allergique' is the same for both genders.
Card 17: the source note on the Spanish double negative (no … nada) corresponds to French 'ne … rien'. This appears in card 17 only, not in the Reader.
Reader lines 7 and 8 are faithful, unqualified translations of the source claims. They are kept verbatim for parity and placed under owner hold (see residuals).

Verb paradigms follow the four source slots in order (comer, estar, tener, usar). The source has five person slots and French has six; the mapping is stated in each explanation. Tener is mapped to 'contenir', not 'avoir', to match Reader line 8.

The Reader has only a Spanish title, 'Desayuno sin carne en Oaxaca', which readerTitleFrench translates. The lesson title 'No, Never and How Much', objective and focus have no French rendering in this candidate.
